source: Deletang et al. (2023) Language Modeling Is Compression
finding: Language models used as arithmetic-coding compressors beat domain-specific compressors on images and audio, even though trained mainly on text.
numbers: Chinchilla 70B: ImageNet patches 43.4% of raw size vs PNG 58.5%; LibriSpeech 16.4% vs FLAC 30.3%. Raw enwik9 rate: Chinchilla 70B 8.3%, Llama 2 7B 8.9%, gzip 32.3%, LZMA2 23.0%.
limits: Raw rate ignores model size. This is the key hidden cost.
agent_relevance: Good prediction equals good compression, so held-out log-loss is a valid MDL score for an LLM hypothesis.

source: Deletang et al. (2023) Language Modeling Is Compression (adjusted rate)
finding: When model parameters are counted as part of the code (two-part code), big foundation models lose. Scaling gains depend on dataset size.
numbers: Adjusted rates for Chinchilla models on ImageNet/LibriSpeech/random are far above 100% (Chinchilla 1B: 194.0 / 146.6 / 195.5). For small Transformers on enwik, each dataset size has a critical model size beyond which the adjusted rate worsens.
limits: Offline setting only. Authors say non-trivial adjusted rates need TB-scale data. Table text was garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: The MDL penalty for model size is real. A scaffold hypothesis should be short relative to the evidence it explains.

source: Deletang et al. (2023) Language Modeling Is Compression (prior knowledge)
finding: Transformers trained from scratch on enwik8 compress only data like their training set; big pretrained models compress other modalities too.
numbers: Transformers 200K/800K/3.2M parameters: enwik9 raw rates 30.9/21.7/17.0, but near 100% on random data and roughly 60-100% on image/audio.
limits: enwik9 is partly out of distribution. Random data stays near 100%, as theory says.
agent_relevance: Compression gains come from prior knowledge, not from the MDL rule alone. The prior matters as much as the length.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Compression Represents Intelligence Linearly
finding: Across 31 public LLMs and 12 benchmarks, bits per character on external raw text correlates linearly with average benchmark score.
numbers: Pearson about -0.95 per domain (knowledge/commonsense, coding, math); overall -0.93 with RMSE 3.1%. Single benchmarks (MMLU, Hellaswag, TriviaQA) about -0.91 to -0.95.
limits: Correlational, base models, limited size range. Needs text the model did not train on.
agent_relevance: Supports a compression-based proxy score for models and candidate hypotheses.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Compression Represents Intelligence Linearly (contamination outlier)
finding: Qwen models were outliers on GSM8K and MATH because of training-data exposure (low Min-K% scores). They were excluded from the fit.
numbers: Three Qwen models scored above the linear-fit prediction on math.
limits: Shows the compression-intelligence line breaks when test text leaks into training.
agent_relevance: Always check held-out status (G3). Compression is gameable by leakage.

source: Grau-Moya et al. (2024) Learning Universal Predictors
finding: Neural nets meta-trained on data from random universal Turing machine programs approximate Solomonoff induction. Larger models do better.
numbers: Regret falls from size S to M to L. Transformer-L reaches optimal regret on variable-order Markov sources (CTW). LSTM-L near optimal. Transformers fail at length generalisation out of distribution while LSTMs do best.
limits: Small synthetic program classes. No claim for real-world data.
agent_relevance: A program prior can be amortised, but length-generalisation limits mean a prompt-only agent cannot assume it.

source: Grau-Moya et al. (2024) Learning Universal Predictors (transfer)
finding: Networks trained on UTM data transfer to Chomsky-hierarchy tasks. Transformer-L is best in-distribution on those tasks.
numbers: Transformer-L best 'by a margin' in cumulative regret and accuracy on in-distribution Chomsky tasks.
limits: Transfer shown only on synthetic algorithmic tasks.
agent_relevance: A simplicity prior learned from programs can help on structured tasks.

source: Ellis et al. (2020) DreamCoder
finding: Wake-sleep library learning that rewards libraries which compress programs solves list, text, graphics and physics domains. Learned abstractions speed search.
numbers: List-function synthesis: 3.7% solved in 10 min before learning, 79.6% after (average search 235 s to 40 s). CVC4 solved 82.4% of the SyGuS set; DreamCoder 84.3% with generous compute. LOGO and tower tasks near 100% held out vs under 60% for any alternative.
limits: Each domain needs about a day on 20-100 CPUs and a hand-built starting language. Tens to hundreds of training tasks.
agent_relevance: Template for S7: compress successful sub-solutions into named reusable operators.

source: Ellis et al. (2020) DreamCoder (ablations)
finding: Both parts matter. Removing library learning (compression) or the neural recognition model lowers solved tasks and raises search time.
numbers: Text-editing mean solve time 54.1 s (median 15.0 s); physics: 93% of laws and identities recovered after 8 wake/sleep cycles.
limits: Ablation only inside this system and its domains.
agent_relevance: Compression and a guided proposer help together; neither alone is enough.

source: Li et al. (2024) Combining Induction and Transduction for Abstract Reasoning
finding: Neural induction (write a program) and transduction (predict the output directly) solve different ARC tasks, even with the same training data and architecture.
numbers: ARC-Potpourri: transduction (TTT, no reranking) 56.75%, reranked 43.0%, induction with 20k samples majority vote 35.25%. ARC-Heavy: transduction TTT 43.25%, induction 19.25%. Best model 56.75% on ARC val vs average human 60.2%, best humans 98%. About 9% of problems fit the training pairs yet miss the test output.
limits: Per-task assignment is stable across seeds, so complementarity is not noise. Transduction often wins on raw rate, so induction does not always win.
agent_relevance: A shortest-program rule needs a direct-answer fallback. Try program search first, answer directly if the budget ends.

source: Li et al. (2024) Combining Induction and Transduction for Abstract Reasoning (ensemble recipe)
finding: Simple ensemble: induction first, checked on training pairs; if no program fits within budget, use transduction.
numbers: Small-compute table: ensemble 26.50% vs induction 18.78% vs transduction 15.25% (one setting); second setting ensemble 19.50% vs induction 11.07% vs transduction 13.50%.
limits: Gains depend on compute budget.
agent_relevance: Checking on the given examples is the filter that separates good programs from bad.

source: Akyurek et al. (2024) The Surprising Effectiveness of Test-Time Training
finding: Updating model weights on the task's own examples at test time raises ARC accuracy a lot over fine-tuned baselines.
numbers: 80 ARC val tasks pass@2: fine-tuned 17.5% to 45.0% with TTT (+27.5 points). 8B model 53.0% on public val; 61.9% when ensembled with program synthesis. BBH 10-shot 50.5% to 57.8% (+7.3).
limits: Needs weight updates and a fine-tuned base. A prompt-only agent cannot do this.
agent_relevance: Fitting the task's own examples matters. In a scaffold the equivalent is leave-one-out checks.

source: Chollet et al. (2025) ARC Prize 2024 Technical Report
finding: ARC Prize 2024 moved the field from brute-force program search to test-time training and LLM-guided program synthesis.
numbers: Private-set top scores: 33% (end 2023) to 55.5% (MindsAI, ineligible); ARChitects 53.5% (TTT); Greenblatt 43% (LLM program sampling); o1-preview 18%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14% pass@1. icecuber brute-force DSL search 20% (2020 contest).
limits: Private set. A human panel solved 99% of public eval tasks (10 workers each).
agent_relevance: LLM program-sampling pipelines had real gains; plain prompting stayed low.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: LM Inductive Reasoning
finding: LMs are strong hypothesis proposers but weak appliers of their own rules. With a symbolic interpreter filtering rules, results are strong.
numbers: Applying their own rules, task accuracy drops from over 80% to almost zero on MiniSCAN. Human baselines: about 80% on one dataset, 45.9% on List Functions, 90.9% on ConceptARC.
limits: Four datasets; the gap is largest where rule use is recursive.
agent_relevance: Run induced rules through an executor, not the model's own reading of them.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: LM Inductive Reasoning (noise)
finding: Hypothesis refinement was tested with 0%, 12.5%, 25% and 50% corrupted examples.
numbers: Noise levels 0, 12.5, 25, 50 percent of examples perturbed. Exact per-level scores are in figures and not copied here.
limits: Figures not read numerically.
agent_relevance: Exact-fit MDL fails with noisy examples. Allow residual error in the code length.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search: Inductive Reasoning with Language Models
finding: Generating abstract hypotheses first, then programs, beats direct prompting on an ARC subset.
numbers: Direct 17%; with abstract hypotheses 23%; with LLM-summarised hypotheses 30%; 33% with human-selected hypotheses. 33 of 49 (67%) tasks with selected hypotheses gave correct programs. SyGuS 94.3% with generated hypotheses.
limits: On 40 questions, human-written hypotheses 47.5% vs 37.5% direct; compositional search helped human hypotheses but hurt model ones.
agent_relevance: Two-stage propose-then-implement is a cheap gain in S2.

source: Grunwald and Roos (2019) Minimum Description Length Revisited
finding: Modern MDL uses luckiness functions instead of strict priors. MDL and Bayes can behave badly under misspecification.
numbers: Review states MDL/Bayes without modification can be sub-optimal when all candidate models are wrong. Also reviews MDL views of deep learning generalisation.
quote: MDL (and Bayes), without modification, can behave sub-optimally under misspecification
limits: Theory review; no experiments.
agent_relevance: Shortest-fit is not safe when the hypothesis class is wrong. Keep a held-out check.

source: Blier and Ollivier (2018) The Description Length of Deep Learning Models
finding: Variational and two-part codes give poor compression for deep nets, but simple prequential (online) coding gives far shorter codes.
numbers: MNIST uniform code 199 kbits; prequential about 4.10 kbits (ratio 0.02) at 99.5% test accuracy; CIFAR10 uniform 166 kbits, prequential about 45.3 kbits.
limits: Digits read from a garbled table. Check the original before reuse.
agent_relevance: Prefer online/prequential cost (predict each next item from earlier ones) as the practical MDL score.

source: Valle-Perez et al. (2019) Deep learning generalizes because the parameter-function map is biased towards simple functions
finding: Random-parameter DNNs prefer simple functions exponentially, as an algorithmic information bound predicts.
numbers: Shown on Boolean functions and on CIFAR10/MNIST with fully connected and convolutional nets; a PAC-Bayes bound over function space.
limits: Complexity estimated with compression proxies. An account of generalisation, not proof about SGD.
agent_relevance: Supports 'simple first' priors but only when target tasks are structured.

source: Mingard et al. (2025) Deep neural networks have an inbuilt Occam's razor
finding: A Bayesian posterior built from a function prior plus likelihood predicts SGD-trained net outcomes. The Occam bias cancels the exponential growth in the number of complex functions.
numbers: Boolean classification; architecture varied between ordered and chaotic regimes; posterior predictions accurate in measured nets.
limits: Boolean tasks and small nets. The prior changes with architecture, so simplicity bias is not universal.
agent_relevance: Simplicity bias depends on architecture; the chaotic regime loses it.

source: Yoran et al. (2025) The Kolmogorov Test: Compression by Code Generation
finding: Code LLMs asked for the shortest program that outputs a sequence do poorly on real data.
numbers: Length-128 zero-shot accuracy: GPT4-O 35.6 (16-bit audio), 15.0 (8-bit audio), 29.6 (MFCC), 24.8 (DNA), 6.5 (text); Llama-3.1-405B 18.0/10.1/24.2/22.5/9.6. Precision above 1 means worse than gzip: GPT4-O 1.66-3.17.
limits: Inputs are raw data sequences, not task rules.
agent_relevance: Frontier models cannot reliably find short programs for real data. Do not trust 'shortest program' claims from the LLM alone.

source: Yoran et al. (2025) The Kolmogorov Test: Compression by Code Generation (synthetic to real)
finding: On synthetic program-sequence pairs, trained SEQCODER beats gzip (precision under 1). Gains do not carry to real audio, DNA or text.
numbers: Synthetic precision 0.56-0.57, accuracy 84.5-92.5 for the best trained rows; near zero on natural data. Models trained on 100K and 1M examples err in the first 16 characters in 93.5% and 88.7% of audio-MFCC length-128 cases.
limits: Trained models of 1.5B and 8B only. Table layout partly garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Program-compression skill does not transfer across distributions; test on real tasks.

source: Gauvrit et al. (2014) Complexity for short strings (coding theorem method)
finding: Standard Kolmogorov complexity fails for short strings (length up to about 50). A coding-theorem estimate from a universal distribution gives an objective measure usable in psychology of randomness.
numbers: Applied to human randomness production and compared with known human biases in sequence generation.
limits: Estimates depend on the reference machine class; short strings only.
agent_relevance: Small observation sets in our tasks need tailored complexity measures, not gzip length.

source: Lake, Salakhutdinov, Tenenbaum (2015) Human-level concept learning through probabilistic program induction (Science)
finding: Bayesian Program Learning matched human one-shot character learning on Omniglot and beat deep networks on one-shot classification.
numbers: From memory only: one-shot error BPL 3.3%, people 4.5%, deep siamese net about 8%; judges could barely tell BPL strokes from human ones.
limits: Not opened this session; check numbers. Needs hand-built stroke primitives.
agent_relevance: Program-like models with a built-in compositional prior beat pattern nets in the very-low-data regime.

source: Feldman (2000) Minimization of Boolean complexity in human concept learning (Nature)
finding: Human difficulty in learning Boolean concepts tracks the length of the shortest logical formula (Boolean complexity).
numbers: From memory only; no figures recorded.
limits: Not opened. Rival accounts exist; not read.
agent_relevance: Human learners lean to short rules, which supports a shortest-fit tie-break in S7.

source: Chater and Vitanyi (2003) Simplicity: a unifying principle in cognitive science? (TICS)
finding: Argues that perception and learning are driven by simplicity, expressed as a shortest-code principle.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Critics say such frameworks can fit any result; not read here.
agent_relevance: Warns against using MDL as a post-hoc story.
